Q: What is a segmentation fault? A:

A segmentation fault is also caused by hardware failures, in this case the RAM memories. This is the less common cause, but if you don't find an error in your code, maybe MemTest86 could help you.

The solution in this case is to change the RAM.

Here there is a reference: Segmentation fault by hardware

Q: How do I resize the PowerShell window in Windows 11 using PowerShell? A:

Indeed, the problem is that if you start powershell.exe directly - rather than from inside WT (Windows Terminal) - the PowerShell process' parent process is explorer.exe - rather than a WindowsTerminal process.

Since it is the WT process that owns the terminal window, the challenge is how to unambiguously identify the specific WT process that in effect hosts the PowerShell session, as Santiago points out.

A solution that is likely robust enough - it relies on WT implementation details, which are unlikely to change, however - is to target the presumably only WT process that has a visible main window:

Add-Type @'
using System;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;

public class Win32 {
  [DllImport("user32.dll")]
  public static extern bool MoveWindow(IntPtr hWnd, int X, int Y, int nWidth, int nHeight, bool bRepaint);
}
'@

[Win32]::MoveWindow(
  (Get-Process -Name WindowsTerminal | Where MainWindowTitle)[-1].MainWindowHandle,
  100, 100, 600, 200, $true
)

Note:

  • This approach works in both invocation scenarios: direct executable invocation with implicit WT launching as well as launching from an existing WT instance, but it does require the PowerShell session to run in a visible WT tab / window.

  • The reason it is sufficient to test for a WindowsTerminal process with a visible main window is as follows:

    • Long-term in a given OS user session it seems that WT only ever maintains one WindowsTerminal process that manages all open tabs and windows, but when wt.exe is used to open a new tab or window, temporarily, briefly there can more than one, namely transient instances that delegate to a preexisting one; you can verify this as follows:

      • From an existing WT tab running PowerShell execute the following:

         Start-Process wt.exe; Start-Sleep -MilliSeconds 20; Get-Process WindowsTerminal

      • This will open a new tab (or window, depending on your configuration); close it to see the results of the submitted command. Typically you'll see two WindowsTerminal instances, whereas executing Get-Process WindowsTerminal again later will only show one.

    • However, only the long-term instance maintains visible window(s), and - should there be multiple windows - .MainWindowHandle / .MainWindowTitle reflect the active WT window's values.[1]

      • Thus, the presumption is that there's only one WindowsTerminal process with valid values in .MainWindowHandle / .MainWindowTitle, and that it represents the only visible instance that manages all the windows.

      • If your powershell.exe process is launched (from outside WT) in a regular desktop session (window station), it will become the active tab / window of either the first WindowsTerminal process to be created or that of a preexisting one. Either way, targeting the applicable process allows manipulating its active window.

Alternatively and robustly - if you control how powershell.exe is invoked - you can call it with wt.exe powershell.exe, in which case WT does become the parent process, and you can use the following code, which reliably identifies the relevant WT process:

# Only for PowerShell sessions started from Windows Terminal or via wt.exe
[Win32]::MoveWindow(
  (Get-Process -Id (Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "ProcessId = $((Get-Process -Id $PID).Id)").ParentProcessId).MainWindowHandle,
  100, 100, 600, 200, $true
)

PowerShell (Core) 7 (pwsh.exe) allows for a more succinct and efficient solution, given that the process objects have a .Parent property there:

# Ditto, but PowerShell (Core) 7 only.
[Win32]::MoveWindow(
  (Get-Process -Id $PID).Parent.MainWindowHandle, 
  100, 100, 600, 200, $true
)

[1] For convenience, Where MainWindowTitle is used, i.e. a test that will return $true if the main window title is a nonempty string. Since WT ignores attempts to set its tab titles to the empty string, this should be robust. If you wanted to test the main window handle, you'd have to use Where MainWindowHandle -ne ([IntPtr]::Zero) - sadly, Where MainWindowHandle is not sufficient, because a null (zero) pointer is unexpectedly not considered "falsy" in PowerShell, and fixing this problem was unfortunately decided against - see GitHub issue #17601.

Q: Why does returning from _start segmentation fault? A:

As per ABI1 the stack at the entry on _start is

There is no "return address".
The only way to exit a process is through SYS_EXIT

xorl %edi, %edi   ;Error code
movl $60, %eax    ;SYS_EXIT
syscall

See also Where is the x86-64 System V ABI documented?

1 Section 3.4.1 Initial Stack and Register State.

Q: Is there a way to track local or foreign users on a website? A:

That's a clever approach. However, my strict constraint is that this tracking needs to happen entirely under the hood without altering the UI or requiring any user interaction. It's strictly for background business logic, so using 'honeypot' links or asking them directly via prompts isn't feasible in my use case. I need to rely purely on silent metadata.
